Sample Size Planning for an ANOVA Contrast From the Accuracy in Parameter Estimation (AIPE) Perspective

Source: R/ss_aipe_c.R
ss_aipe_c.Rd

Plans the sample size per group so that the confidence interval for an unstandardized contrast of means in a fixed effects analysis of variance is sufficiently narrow, following the accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) approach: the design goal is a contrast estimated with the precision the research question requires, not merely one detected as nonzero. AIPE sample size planning for ANOVA and ANCOVA contrasts is developed in Lai and Kelley (2012).

Usage

ss_aipe_c(
  true_var_error,
  c_weights,
  width,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  assurance = NULL,
  true_kurtosis = 0
)

Arguments

true_var_error

The population error variance: the variance of the errors common to the groups, which the mean square error (the mean square within groups) of an analysis of variance estimates. It is a variance, not a standard deviation: a planning value stated as an error standard deviation is squared before it is given. Must be a single finite positive number. This is the one way to state the error variability, as in ss_aipe_c_sensitivity and ss_power_contrast.

c_weights

The contrast weights

width

The desired full width of the obtained confidence interval

conf_level

The desired confidence interval coverage, (i.e., 1 - Type I error rate). A level above .999999998, whose tail areas are below 1e-9, is refused (see "Small tail areas" in ci_nc_t).

assurance

Parameter to ensure that the obtained confidence interval width is narrower than the desired width with a specified degree of certainty (must be NULL or between zero and unity)

true_kurtosis

The population excess kurtosis of the errors (their fourth standardized moment less 3), on the scale kurtosis reports, so the value it gives for the residuals of a pilot study can be passed directly. It is used only with assurance, through the effective degrees of freedom described in Details: a negative value (lighter tails than the normal, as bounded outcomes such as proportions and rating scale scores often have) makes the sample variance less variable than normal theory implies, and a positive value (heavier tails) makes it more variable. The default 0 is the normal theory value. Must be a single finite number greater than -2; no distribution has a smaller excess kurtosis, and only a symmetric two-point distribution attains -2.

Value

A 1-row data.frame with columns term and value:

necessary_n_per_group

the necessary sample size per group

A plan made with assurance and a nonzero true_kurtosis keeps that one row, carries the value as the attribute true_kurtosis, prints a line under the table saying that the assurance allows for that excess kurtosis of the errors, and reports it as a true_kurtosis column of generics::glance(). With the default true_kurtosis = 0, or without assurance, no attribute is added.

Details

Without assurance, the planned n per group is the smallest integer (and at least 2) satisfying $$n \ge \frac{4\, t^2_{1-\alpha/2,\, J(n-1)}\, \sigma^2 \sum_j c_j^2}{\omega^2},$$ where \(\sigma^2\) is the error variance (true_var_error), \(c_j\) are the contrast weights of the \(J\) groups, and \(\omega\) is the desired full width. That is the width the interval would have if the pooled sample variance \(S^2\) equaled \(\sigma^2\); because \(S^2\) varies from sample to sample, the realized width exceeds \(\omega\) in a large proportion of studies, a proportion that approaches one half as n grows. With assurance equal to \(\gamma\), the right side is multiplied by \(\chi^2_{\gamma,\, \nu} / \nu\), the \(\gamma\) quantile of a chi square on \(\nu\) degrees of freedom divided by \(\nu\), which is the \(\gamma\) quantile of \(S^2/\sigma^2\) when \(\nu S^2/\sigma^2\) is chi square on \(\nu\) degrees of freedom; the realized width is then at most \(\omega\) with probability \(\gamma\). For normal errors \(\nu = J(n - 1)\) and the chi square law is exact.

For errors that are not normal, the variability of \(S^2\) depends on their excess kurtosis \(\kappa\). With \(J\) groups of \(n\), the pooled variance has \(\mathrm{var}(S^2) = \sigma^4 [2/\{J(n - 1)\} + \kappa/(nJ)]\), so, for an assurance above one half, a plan made under normality delivers more assurance than requested when \(\kappa < 0\) and less when \(\kappa > 0\). The true_kurtosis argument replaces \(J(n - 1)\) in the chi square quantile with the effective degrees of freedom $$\nu = \frac{2}{2/\{J(n - 1)\} + \kappa/(nJ)},$$ the degrees of freedom for which \(\chi^2_\nu/\nu\) has the variance of \(S^2/\sigma^2\); \(\kappa = 0\) gives \(\nu = J(n - 1)\) and the normal theory plan, and the degrees of freedom of the t quantile are not changed. This is the approximation of Box (1953, p. 319, Eq. 3): a variance estimate on \(\phi\) degrees of freedom from a population with excess kurtosis \(\gamma_2\) has variance \(2\sigma^4/(d\phi)\), with \(d = [1 + \phi\gamma_2/\{2(\phi + 1)\}]^{-1}\), and is distributed approximately as a normal theory estimate on \(d\phi\) degrees of freedom; with \(\phi = n - 1\) in each group, \(\nu\) is \(d\) times \(J(n - 1)\). The approximation matches two moments and leaves the shape to the chi square. It requires errors with a finite fourth moment, and in Box's sampling experiments (p. 325) the large sample result was approached more slowly when the kurtosis was large. The kurtosis of a pilot study's residuals is itself an imprecise estimate in samples of the size pilots have, so the value supplied is a planning value, as the error variance is. The sensitivity companion, ss_aipe_c_sensitivity, simulates normal errors and has no true_kurtosis argument, so it evaluates a plan under the normal theory law, not under the errors a nonzero true_kurtosis allows for.

A Monte Carlo check of the approximation used two groups, c_weights = c(1, -1), an error variance of 1, a width of .8, and an assurance of .80, with 10,000 replications per condition. With uniform errors (excess kurtosis -1.2), the plan made with the kurtosis supplied (53 per group) met the width target in a proportion .811 of the replications, where the plan made under normality (55 per group) met it in .915; with t errors on 10 degrees of freedom (excess kurtosis 1), the plan with the kurtosis supplied (56 per group) met it in .811, where the normal theory plan (55 per group) met it in .776, short of the .80 requested. The study's script and results are kept with the package's development records and are not distributed with the package.

Note

Be sure to use the error variance and not its square root (i.e., the standard deviation of the errors).

References

Box, G. E. P. (1953). Non-normality and tests on variances. Biometrika, 40(3–4), 318–335. doi:10.1093/biomet/40.3-4.318

Kelley, K., Maxwell, S. E., & Rausch, J. R. (2003). Obtaining power or obtaining precision: Delineating methods of sample-size planning. Evaluation & the Health Professions, 26(3), 258–287. doi:10.1177/0163278703255242

Lai, K., & Kelley, K. (2012). Accuracy in parameter estimation for ANCOVA and ANOVA contrasts: Sample size planning via narrow confidence intervals. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 65, 350–370. doi:10.1111/j.2044-8317.2011.02029.x

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

See also

ss_aipe_sc, ss_aipe_c_ancova, ci_c

design_consequences for what a chosen design delivers: power, the Type S (sign) and Type M (exaggeration) errors of the significance filter, and the expected confidence interval width.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Suppose the population error variance of some three-group ANOVA model
# is believed to be 40. The researcher is interested in the difference
# between the mean of group 1 and the average of means of group 2 and 3.
# To plan the sample size so that, with 90 percent certainty, the
# obtained 95 percent full confidence interval width is no wider than 3:

ss_aipe_c(true_var_error = 40, c_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),
          width = 3, assurance = .90)
#>  term                  value
#>  necessary_n_per_group 114  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The planning values can come from a pilot study. The posttest scores in
# depression_bdi have an error variance near 40, and their residuals are
# lighter tailed than the normal, as scores on a bounded inventory often
# are. Thirty residuals estimate the kurtosis imprecisely, so it is a
# planning value to weigh, as the error variance is.
pilot <- lm(bdi_post ~ condition, data = depression_bdi)
sigma(pilot)^2
#> [1] 39.61852
kurtosis(residuals(pilot))
#> [1] -0.9045304
ss_aipe_c(true_var_error = sigma(pilot)^2, c_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),
          width = 3, assurance = .90, true_kurtosis = kurtosis(residuals(pilot)))
#>  term                  value
#>  necessary_n_per_group 110  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> The assurance allows for errors with an excess kurtosis of -0.905 (normal errors have 0).
